<main class="talk">

<section class="section hero" id="benqodhi">
<div>
<div class="eyebrow">JRC Ispra | 10-11 September 2026</div>
<h1>BENQODHI</h1>
<div class="subtitle">
BENchmarking Quantum Optimization:<br>
from Datasets to Health Innovation
</div>
<div class="one-line">From Bengodi to benchmarks: promises need evidence.</div>
</div>

<figure class="image-frame">
<img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/04/Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Land_of_Cockaigne_-_WGA3507.jpg" alt="Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Land of Cockaigne">
<figcaption>Bruegel, <em>The Land of Cockaigne</em>, 1567. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>

<section class="section" id="why-now">
<div class="eyebrow">Why now</div>
<h2>A moment when AI, quantum computing and scientific benchmarking are forced to talk to each other</h2>
<p class="lead">
AI is already changing scientific work. Quantum computing is a strategic possibility. The useful question is not who wins, but how we compare claims on common problems.
</p>

<div class="news-grid">
<div class="news-card">
<div class="date">Research signal | 8 September 2026</div>
<h3>OpenAI reports an AI-generated Navier-Stokes result</h3>
<p>OpenAI says an internal multi-agent system produced a proof with a Lean formalization, using on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents for the Navier-Stokes effort.</p>
<p>This is exactly why formulation matters: problem statement, assumptions, verification, cost and community validation become part of the scientific object.</p>
<div class="source-note"><a href="https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/">OpenAI announcement</a></div>
</div>

<div class="cue-grid" style="margin-top: 0;">
<div class="cue">
<h3>AI</h3>
<p>Models, agents, search, coding, summarization and experimental support.</p>
</div>
<div class="cue">
<h3>Quantum</h3>
<p>Optimization, sampling, simulation and hybrid algorithms.</p>
</div>
<div class="cue">
<h3>Evidence</h3>
<p>Common tasks, strong baselines, transparent resources and reproducible comparisons.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>

<section class="section" id="benchmarking">
<div class="eyebrow">Benchmarking</div>
<h2>A benchmark is a protocol, not only a dataset</h2>
<p class="lead">
The point is to reduce cherry-picking and make progress comparable across classical, AI, quantum and hybrid approaches.
</p>

<div class="benchmark-flow">
<div class="metric">
<h3>Problem</h3>
<p>Scientific meaning and mathematical formulation.</p>
</div>
<div class="metric">
<h3>Instances</h3>
<p>Data, generators, regimes of difficulty and documented structure.</p>
</div>
<div class="metric">
<h3>Baselines</h3>
<p>Classical, AI, quantum and hybrid methods compared fairly.</p>
</div>
<div class="metric">
<h3>Metrics</h3>
<p>Quality, accuracy, uncertainty, robustness and domain relevance.</p>
</div>
<div class="metric">
<h3>Resources</h3>
<p>Runtime, hardware, energy, data, tuning and human effort.</p>
</div>
<div class="metric">
<h3>Repository</h3>
<p>Reusable evidence, not isolated demonstrations.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="flow-arrow">problem formulation -> comparable evidence -> shared repository</div>
</section>

<section class="section" id="work-streams">
<div class="eyebrow">Two work streams</div>
<h2>Controlled problems and real bottlenecks</h2>

<div class="streams">
<article class="stream">
<img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fe/2D_ising_model_on_lattice.svg" alt="Two-dimensional Ising model lattice">
<div class="source-note">Ta2o, 2D Ising model lattice, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.</div>
<h3>Controlled optimization</h3>
<p>Sapienza collaboration: theoretical instances, especially spin-glass-style problems, with contact points to real hard optimization.</p>
<ul>
<li>clean enough to measure performance</li>
<li>structured enough to study difficulty</li>
<li>shared repository to avoid cherry-picking</li>
</ul>
</article>

<article class="stream">
<img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f7/DNA_sequencing_interferogram.png" alt="DNA sequencing interferogram">
<div class="source-note">NHGRI, DNA sequencing trace, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.</div>
<h3>Health and life sciences</h3>
<p>A scan of real bottlenecks where AI, quantum or hybrid methods could make a difference in coming years.</p>
<ul>
<li>genomics, imaging, mechanistic biology, clinical and operational tasks</li>
<li>portfolio approach, also reusing existing benchmarks</li>
<li>not limited to quantum-only solutions</li>
</ul>
</article>
</div>
</section>

<section class="section" id="workshop-output">
<div class="eyebrow">Workshop output</div>
<h2>Not a final product: a shared formulation exercise</h2>
<p class="lead">
Today gives us the landscape. Tomorrow we try to turn it into candidate benchmark problems, repository criteria and policy questions.
</p>

<div class="roundtables">
<div>
<strong>Tables 1-3</strong>
Candidate benchmark problems in health and life-science domains.
</div>
<div>
<strong>Table 4</strong>
How to compare quantum, AI, hybrid and classical approaches.
</div>
<div>
<strong>Table 5</strong>
Infrastructure, indicators, investment and policy relevance.
</div>
</div>

<div class="output-strip">
<span>candidate problems</span>
<span>reusable benchmarks</span>
<span>repository criteria</span>
<span>policy implications</span>
</div>

<p class="closing">
The goal is to find good problems, and formulate them well enough that others can solve them.
</p>
</section>
